source.title: Think and Grow Rich
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of Think and Grow Rich by Napoleon Hill (1937). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright. Cards cover only the book's practical ideas (definite goals, planning, persistence, the mastermind group, decisiveness, specialised knowledge); its claims about autosuggestion and thoughts attracting wealth are not presented.

cards.title: Vague hopes go nowhere; a definite, written goal gives you direction
cards.body:
Hill's starting point is that most people never decide exactly what they want. They hope for "more" without saying how much, by when, or what they will give in return.

He urges you to name a specific aim, set a date for it, decide what you will offer to earn it and write it all down. The value is practical: a clear target tells you which opportunities matter, which to ignore and how to judge your progress. A goal you can state in one sentence is far easier to act on than a wish.
cards.apply_it: Write one goal as a single sentence with a specific amount or outcome, a deadline, and what you will do or give to reach it.

quiz.question: What does Hill say most people lack?
quiz.explanation: Without a clearly stated aim, effort has no direction and progress cannot be judged.

cards.title: When a plan fails, treat it as a flawed plan, not a final defeat
cards.body:
Hill argues that a goal needs a practical plan behind it, and that first plans are often weak. When one does not work, he says, the sensible response is to replace it with a better plan, not to abandon the goal.

He treats setbacks as temporary rather than as proof you were wrong to try. Many people quit at the first failure, so simply revising and trying again puts you ahead. In modern terms it is iteration: test, learn what went wrong, adjust and go again.
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you dropped after a setback. Write down why the plan failed and one changed approach you could try instead.

quiz.question: How does Hill suggest you respond when a plan fails?
options: Replace it with a new, better plan while keeping the goal
quiz.explanation: Hill saw failure as temporary defeat of a plan, not of the goal itself.

cards.title: Persistence is what separates people who reach goals from those who don't
cards.body:
Hill gives a great deal of weight to sheer persistence. In his view, most people have the ability to achieve more, but they drift away when progress is slow or criticism arrives.

He treats persistence as something you can build: a clear goal you care about, a concrete plan, friends who encourage you and the habit of acting every day all make it easier to keep going. Willpower alone fades; structure and support help it last. Persistence is not stubbornness about methods, though. It is staying with the aim while changing tactics.
cards.apply_it: Pick one goal and commit to a small action toward it every day this week, even on days you feel unmotivated.

quiz.question: According to Hill, what helps build persistence?
options: Keeping your goal secret from everyone
A clear goal, a plan, supportive people and daily action
Avoiding all plans so you stay flexible
quiz.explanation: He saw persistence as supported by structure and people, not just raw willpower.

cards.title: Build a small group of people who help each other toward their goals
cards.body:
Hill's best-known practical idea is the "mastermind": two or more people who meet regularly and work together in a spirit of harmony toward a shared aim, or to help each member with theirs.

No one has all the knowledge, skill or contacts they need. A trusted group pools experience, spots blind spots, offers accountability and keeps morale up. The key ingredients are commitment and goodwill; a group full of rivalry or cynicism does more harm than good. Today this looks like peer advisory groups, accountability partners or a small circle of founders.
cards.apply_it: Name two or three people with goals similar to yours and invite them to a monthly call to share progress and problems.

quiz.question: What is a 'mastermind' in Hill's sense?
options: A group working together in harmony toward goals
quiz.explanation: Hill described it as people cooperating harmoniously and pooling knowledge and effort.

cards.title: Make decisions promptly and change them only for good reason
cards.body:
Hill observed that successful people tended to reach decisions quickly and stick with them, while those who struggled were slow to decide and quick to reverse course. He saw indecision as a close relative of procrastination.

He also warned against letting other people's opinions decide for you. Gather useful facts, then trust your own judgment. The modern lesson is that delay is itself a choice with costs: most decisions are reversible, and acting on a reasonable choice usually beats waiting for certainty that never comes.
cards.apply_it: Pick one decision you've been putting off. Set a deadline of 24 hours, gather the key facts, and decide.

quiz.question: What pattern did Hill associate with failure?
options: Deciding slowly and changing decisions often
Deciding quickly and sticking with it
quiz.explanation: He linked slow, easily reversed decisions to failure and prompt, firm ones to success.

cards.title: General knowledge doesn't pay; organised, specialised knowledge used toward a goal does
cards.body:
Hill argues that knowing lots of facts is not enough to earn well. What counts is specialised knowledge, organised into a plan and applied toward a definite end.

You don't need to hold it all yourself. He points out that you can draw on experts, advisers and your mastermind group, and that adults can keep learning through courses and study long after school. The useful question is not "how much do I know?" but "what specific knowledge does my goal require, and where can I get it?"
cards.apply_it: For your main goal, list the specific knowledge it requires. Mark which you have, and name a person or course for one gap.

quiz.question: What kind of knowledge does Hill say leads to results?
options: Specialised knowledge organised and applied toward a goal
Knowledge you keep entirely to yourself
quiz.explanation: Knowledge pays only when it is specific, organised into a plan and put to use.

cards.title: Commit fully by removing your easy way back
cards.body:
Hill tells of a commander who burned his own ships after landing his army, so retreat was impossible and the only option left was to win. He uses the story to argue that people succeed more often when they commit wholeheartedly instead of keeping one foot out of the door.

You don't need to take reckless risks to use this. It can mean paying for the course up front, telling your mentor your deadline or deleting the distracting app. Small steps that make quitting harder help you follow through when motivation dips.
cards.apply_it: Pick one goal and take one action today that makes backing out a little harder, such as booking, paying or telling someone.

quiz.question: What is the point of Hill's story about burning the ships?
options: Removing the easy way back strengthens commitment
Plans should always have a backup
quiz.explanation: With no retreat available, the army had to commit fully. Hill uses it to show the power of wholehearted commitment.

cards.title: Many people quit just short of success
cards.body:
Hill tells the story of R. U. Darby, whose uncle's gold mine seemed to run dry. They sold the equipment cheaply and went home. The buyer consulted a mining engineer and found the vein just three feet from where they had stopped digging.

Darby later said the lesson made him a better salesman: he stopped treating the first 'no' as final. Hill's point is that setbacks often arrive just before a breakthrough. Before giving up, it is worth asking whether you have really run out of options, or simply out of patience, and whether an expert could see what you are missing.
cards.apply_it: Think of something you nearly gave up on. Who is one expert you could ask before deciding to stop?

quiz.question: What did the buyer of Darby's mine do differently?
options: Dug in a completely new place
Consulted a mining engineer and found the vein close by
quiz.explanation: The buyer sought expert advice and found the gold just three feet away, where Darby had stopped.

cards.title: Start close to where you want to be, even in a humble role
cards.body:
Hill tells of Edwin C. Barnes, who was determined to become Thomas Edison's business partner. With little money and no connections, he travelled to Edison's laboratory and took an ordinary job there, working for years without any obvious progress toward his aim.

The practical lesson is that getting near the people and work you care about can matter more than starting at the top. A junior role, an internship or volunteering in the right place lets you learn, build trust and be ready when an opening appears.
cards.apply_it: Where would you most like to work or who would you most like to learn from? What humble way in could you try?

quiz.question: How did Edwin Barnes first get close to Thomas Edison?
options: He bought shares in Edison's company
He took an ordinary job at Edison's laboratory
quiz.explanation: Barnes started in a modest role, which put him in the right place when an opportunity came.

cards.title: Opportunity often turns up looking like unglamorous work
cards.body:
When Edison's company produced a new dictating machine, Hill recounts, the salesmen weren't keen on it. Barnes saw his chance, said he could sell it, and did so well that he won the selling rights and the partnership he had wanted.

Hill's lesson is that opportunity rarely announces itself. It often appears as a task nobody else wants, a product that seems hard to sell or a problem others avoid. Volunteering for it can show what you can do and open doors that a comfortable task never would.
cards.apply_it: Is there a task or project at your work that others avoid? Consider offering to take it on.

quiz.question: How did Barnes's big opportunity arrive, according to Hill?
options: A product the salesmen weren't keen on, which he offered to sell
A promotion based on years of service
quiz.explanation: Barnes seized a task others had little enthusiasm for, and it led to his partnership with Edison.

cards.title: Most new ideas are old ideas combined in a new way
cards.body:
Hill describes what he calls synthetic imagination: the ability to take existing ideas, methods or products and arrange them into new combinations. He saw this as the source of most inventions and business ideas.

This is a practical and encouraging view of creativity. You don't need a flash of genius from nowhere. Combining a service that works in one city with a need you see in another, or joining two skills you already have, can create something genuinely useful.
cards.apply_it: List three skills you have and three problems you see around you. Try pairing them up into a possible idea.

quiz.question: What does Hill mean by 'synthetic imagination'?
options: Rearranging existing ideas into new combinations
Imagining things that can never exist
quiz.explanation: Synthetic imagination combines existing ideas and methods in new ways, which Hill saw as the root of most invention.

cards.title: An idea's value depends on what someone does with it
cards.body:
Hill tells how an old country doctor sold a kettle and a secret drink formula to a young drug clerk for a modest sum. In the hands of Asa Candler, that formula became Coca-Cola.

The doctor had the idea; the clerk added vision, effort and selling. Hill's point is that an idea by itself is worth little. Its value comes from the plan, work and persistence that turn it into something people want. Today, many people have similar ideas; the ones who succeed are usually those who act on them.
cards.apply_it: Write down one idea you've had for a while. What is the very first concrete step to test it?

quiz.question: What does Hill's Coca-Cola story suggest about ideas?
options: An idea's value comes from the action and plan behind it
You should never sell an idea
quiz.explanation: The formula became valuable only once someone added vision, effort and selling to it.

cards.title: Being a good follower is how most leaders begin
cards.body:
Hill observes that most leaders started out as followers, and that there is no shame in following. The best followers, he says, become leaders because they learn from those they follow and develop their abilities along the way.

This is reassuring if you are early in your career. Doing a junior role well, with attention and a willingness to learn, is not wasted time. It is how you build the understanding of people and work that leadership later requires.
cards.apply_it: In your current role, what is one thing your manager does well that you could learn from this week?

quiz.question: What is Hill's view of being a follower?
options: It's a sign you'll never lead
Followers should avoid learning from leaders
Most leaders began as followers who learned well
quiz.explanation: Hill says intelligent followers learn from their leaders and often become leaders themselves.

cards.title: Leadership rests on courage, fairness and taking responsibility
cards.body:
Hill lists qualities he saw in effective leaders. Among them: steady courage, self-control, a strong sense of justice, firm decisions, clear plans, doing more than you are paid for, mastery of detail, sympathy for others and willingness to take full responsibility, including for followers' mistakes.

The list still holds up. Notice that most of the qualities are about character and habits, not charisma. They can be practised by anyone, whether you lead a team, a family or a community group.
cards.apply_it: Choose one quality from Hill's list that you're weakest in, and pick one small way to practise it this week.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the leadership qualities Hill lists?
quiz.explanation: Hill includes willingness to assume full responsibility, even for followers' mistakes, among the traits of a good leader.

cards.title: Leaders fail when they lean on title instead of service
cards.body:
Hill also lists reasons leaders fail. They include poor organisation of detail, being unwilling to do humble work, expecting to be paid for what they know rather than what they do with it, fearing that followers may outshine them, selfishness and leaning on authority or title to command respect.

The common thread is ego. A good leader trains people who might one day surpass them, rolls up their sleeves when needed and earns respect through usefulness. Pulling rank is usually a sign that real leadership is missing.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel tempted to say 'because I said so', try explaining your reasons instead.

quiz.question: Which of these does Hill name as a cause of failure in leadership?
quiz.explanation: Hill lists fear of followers' competition, reliance on title and unwillingness to do humble work among common failings.

cards.title: Lead with people's consent, not by force
cards.body:
Hill distinguishes two kinds of leadership: leadership by force and leadership by consent, with the goodwill of the people being led. He argues that leadership imposed by force cannot last, while leadership people willingly accept is far stronger.

This applies well beyond politics. A manager who only uses threats gets minimum effort and quick exits. A parent, teacher or team lead who explains, listens and earns trust gets cooperation that lasts. Respect that is earned outlives authority that is imposed.
cards.apply_it: Think of a time you were led well. What did that person do that made you want to follow?

quiz.question: Which kind of leadership does Hill say lasts longer?
options: Leadership by consent of the followers
quiz.explanation: Hill argues leadership people willingly accept outlasts leadership imposed by force.

cards.title: Judge your work by its quality, quantity and spirit
cards.body:
Hill offers a simple formula for anyone selling their services, whether as an employee or self-employed. He calls it QQS: the quality of your work, the quantity of it, and the spirit in which you do it. He adds that doing more and better work than you are paid for builds a reputation that leads to better pay.

The 'spirit' part is easy to overlook. A cooperative, positive attitude often matters as much as skill when people decide whom to promote, hire again or recommend.
cards.apply_it: Rate yourself from 1 to 5 on quality, quantity and spirit at work. Pick the lowest and improve it this week.

quiz.question: What do the letters in Hill's QQS formula stand for?
quiz.explanation: Hill's QQS formula covers the quality and quantity of service, and the spirit of cooperation behind it.

cards.title: When seeking work, present a clear written case for yourself
cards.body:
Hill advises people looking for a job to prepare a careful written summary, which he calls a brief, setting out their education, experience and references, and naming the specific position they want rather than asking for 'any job'.

The principle carries straight over to modern CVs and applications. Tailor what you send to the role, show what you can do for the employer, and be specific about the job you're aiming for. A focused application tells the reader you've thought about their needs, not just your own.
cards.apply_it: Pick one job you'd like and rewrite the top of your CV so it speaks directly to that role.

quiz.question: What does Hill advise when applying for a job?
options: Ask for any job that's available
Name the specific position and present a clear written case
Send the same letter to everyone
quiz.explanation: Hill recommends naming the exact position you want and backing it with a well-prepared written summary.

cards.title: Choose work you can like, not only work that pays
cards.body:
Among Hill's causes of failure is choosing the wrong occupation. He argues that no one does their best in work they dislike, and that liking your field makes the effort and persistence that success needs far easier.

This doesn't mean you must love every job or quit to follow a passion. Many people have to take what is available. But when you do have choices, interest and fit deserve weight alongside pay, and you can steer gradually toward work that suits you.
cards.apply_it: List the parts of your current work you enjoy most. How could you do more of them over the next year?

quiz.question: Why does Hill think choosing work you like matters?
options: People rarely do their best in work they dislike
You should always quit jobs you don't love
quiz.explanation: Hill argues liking your work makes sustained effort and persistence much easier.

cards.title: Take an honest personal inventory at least once a year
cards.body:
Hill provides a long self-analysis questionnaire and suggests going through it regularly, at least yearly. The questions ask things like whether you reached this year's goal, whether you gave your best effort, whether you wasted time, and whether your habits and attitude helped or hurt you.

The value lies in honesty. A regular review shows patterns you can't see day to day, such as procrastination or drifting focus, and lets you correct course before another year passes.
cards.apply_it: Set a date in your calendar for a yearly self-review. Start with three questions: what went well, what didn't, what will I change?

quiz.question: How often does Hill suggest doing a personal inventory?
quiz.explanation: Hill recommends a regular self-analysis, at least yearly, to spot patterns and correct course.

cards.title: Beware the desire to get something for nothing
cards.body:
Hill lists the urge to get something for nothing among the major causes of failure. He points to the gambling mood that drove many people to speculate wildly in the stock market before the 1929 crash, and lose heavily.

The lesson fits today's world of betting apps, crypto hype and 'double your money' schemes. Real wealth usually comes from giving value, through work, skills or a business, and from patient saving and investing. When the main appeal is a big win with little effort, the odds are usually against you.
cards.apply_it: Look at your last month's spending. How much went on betting or get-rich-quick schemes? Could it go toward savings instead?

quiz.question: What example does Hill give of the 'something for nothing' urge?
options: Saving a fixed part of income
Speculating wildly before the 1929 stock market crash
quiz.explanation: Hill points to the gambling mood before the 1929 crash as an example of chasing gains without giving value.

cards.title: Get the facts instead of guessing
cards.body:
Another failure Hill lists is guessing instead of thinking. He notes that many people form opinions or make decisions based on hearsay and assumptions, simply because finding out the facts takes effort.

Today, rumours and misleading headlines travel faster than ever. Before a big money, career or health decision, it pays to check the source, ask someone who knows, and separate what you actually know from what you've assumed. A little effort to get the facts can save a great deal of regret.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important decision, write two lists: what I know for sure, and what I'm assuming. Check one assumption.

quiz.question: What does Hill mean by 'guessing instead of thinking'?
options: Deciding on hearsay and assumptions instead of facts
quiz.explanation: Hill criticises forming opinions on assumptions and rumours when the facts could be found.

cards.title: Choose the people you do business with carefully
cards.body:
Hill names the wrong choice of business associates as a common cause of failure. He stresses the importance of choosing an employer or partner who is capable, honest and worth learning from, because you tend to absorb the habits and standards of the people you work closely with.

This matters whether you are picking a boss, a co-founder or a supplier. Skills can be learned, but poor character in a partner tends to cost you sooner or later. Check track records and ask people who have worked with them.
cards.apply_it: Before your next partnership or job, talk to one person who has worked with them before. Ask what they're like under pressure.

quiz.question: Why does Hill stress choosing associates carefully?
options: You tend to absorb the habits and standards of those you work with
Because you should always work alone
quiz.explanation: Hill argues the people you work with shape your habits and standards, so choose them well.

cards.title: Keep your plans close until results can speak
cards.body:
Hill warns that sharing your plans widely invites a flood of opinions, and that friends and relatives, without meaning harm, can discourage you or even ridicule your ideas. He suggests confiding in a small, trusted circle and otherwise letting your actions show what you intended.

This is different from making decisions quickly; it is about protecting a fragile plan in its early stages. Talking about a goal can also feel like progress when it isn't. Showing results tends to carry more weight than announcing intentions.
cards.apply_it: Choose one plan you've been talking about. Tell only one trusted person, and focus on a result you can show.

quiz.question: Why does Hill suggest keeping plans to a small trusted circle?
options: Secrecy is always necessary in business
Wide sharing invites discouraging opinions that can derail you
quiz.explanation: Well-meaning opinions and ridicule can discourage you early, so Hill suggests sharing only with trusted allies.

cards.title: Guard your outlook against constant negativity
cards.body:
Hill warns that people can absorb discouragement from those around them without noticing. Repeated cynicism, sneering at ambition or constant talk of failure can slowly wear down your confidence.

His remedy is partly awareness and partly choice: notice whose comments leave you deflated, spend more time with people who encourage you, and don't hand your judgement over to every critic. You can still love people who are negative while limiting how much their outlook shapes yours.
cards.apply_it: List the three people you talk to most. After each conversation this week, note whether you felt lifted or drained.

quiz.question: What does Hill suggest about negative influences?
options: Cut off anyone who disagrees with you
They have no effect on you
Argue with them until they change
Notice them and choose to spend more time with encouraging people
quiz.explanation: Hill suggests awareness and choosing encouraging company, without needing to cut everyone off.

cards.title: Fear of criticism quietly kills initiative
cards.body:
Hill describes fear of criticism as one of the basic fears holding people back. It shows up as shyness, conforming to what others expect, avoiding risks and not putting forward your ideas, often because of what relatives, friends or colleagues might say.

Naming this fear helps. Much criticism is passing and says more about the critic than about you. Asking 'what is the worst likely reaction, and could I live with it?' often shows that the cost of trying is smaller than the cost of staying silent.
cards.apply_it: Think of one idea you've held back for fear of what people will say. Share it with one supportive person this week.

quiz.question: According to Hill, what does fear of criticism often lead to?
options: Conformity and a lack of initiative
quiz.explanation: Hill says fear of criticism makes people conform and avoid putting their ideas forward.

cards.title: Fear of poverty can show up as worry, doubt and endless delay
cards.body:
Hill names fear of poverty as one of the most destructive fears. He lists its symptoms: indifference, indecision, doubt, worry, too much caution and procrastination.

It can seem odd that a fear of being poor would keep people poor, but the pattern is familiar. Worry about money can freeze you into never starting the business, never asking for the raise, never making a decision. Recognising the fear behind the delay is the first step to deciding calmly and acting.
cards.apply_it: Pick one money decision you've been delaying. Write down what you fear, then the smallest safe step you could take.

quiz.question: Which of these does Hill list as a symptom of the fear of poverty?
quiz.explanation: Hill lists indecision, doubt, worry, over-caution and procrastination as signs of this fear.

cards.title: Watch for the excuses that keep you stuck
cards.body:
Hill ends his chapter on fear with a long list of common excuses, each beginning with 'if': if I had money, if I had a better education, if I had the time, if people understood me. He suggests that people often cling to these alibis to explain why they haven't acted.

Circumstances are real, and some obstacles are serious. But noticing your favourite 'if' helps you separate genuine barriers from comfortable excuses. Then you can ask what is possible even with things as they are.
cards.apply_it: Finish this sentence honestly: 'I would do it if...'. Then ask what small part you could do anyway.

quiz.question: What is the common word at the start of the excuses Hill lists?
quiz.explanation: Hill's list of alibis all begin with 'if', such as 'if I had money' or 'if I had time'.

cards.title: A closed mind shuts out opportunity
cards.body:
Hill includes superstition and prejudice among the causes of failure, and argues that successful people keep open minds. Fixed, unexamined beliefs about people, ideas or what is possible stop you from noticing chances and learning from others.

This matters in a fast-changing world. Dismissing a new technology, a different culture or an unfamiliar method without looking into it can cost you opportunities. Staying curious and willing to change your view is a practical advantage, not just a virtue.
cards.apply_it: Think of an idea or group you've dismissed without really looking into it. Spend ten minutes learning about it.

quiz.question: Why does Hill list prejudice as a cause of failure?
options: It makes you work too hard
Fixed, unexamined beliefs stop you seeing opportunities
quiz.explanation: A closed mind blocks learning and the opportunities that come with it.

cards.title: Decide that worry isn't worth its price
cards.body:
Hill suggests that worry is fed by indecision, and that one way to master it is to make a firm, general decision that nothing in life is worth the price of constant worry. Once you have decided, he says, peace of mind follows more easily.

The practical heart of this is that worry often circles around things you haven't decided or can't control. Making a decision, even a small one, or accepting that something is out of your hands can break the loop. It is not a cure for anxiety, but it is a useful habit of mind.
cards.apply_it: Write down one worry. Next to it, write either a decision you can make about it, or 'out of my control'.

quiz.question: What does Hill suggest feeds worry?
quiz.explanation: Hill links worry to indecision; making a decision or accepting what you can't control can loosen it.
